query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the powder metallurgy route by using controlled mechanical alloying (approximately 10 hours using high-purity milling media and an inert atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (with precisely controlled temperature and time) will yield a uniform, nanocrystalline refractory HEA structure that significantly improves both yield strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory HEAs produced by conventional melting methods, typically characterized by coarse grains and a brittle, albeit strong, behavior at ambient temperatures.
generation.intervention: Adopt an optimized powder metallurgy process featuring approximately 10 hours of mechanical alloying under inert conditions followed by spark plasma sintering with well-tuned sintering parameters.
generation.conditions: Mechanical alloying must be performed in an inert atmosphere with high-purity media to minimize contamination, and spark plasma sintering should be carried out under controlled temperature (e.g., around 1150°C) and short hold times to prevent undesirable phase formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, ultrafine equiaxed grain structure with a high density of beneficial grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement enhances yield strength via the Hall–Petch effect. Furthermore, the increased grain boundary area provides alternative pathways for dislocation movement, thereby enhancing ductility while maintaining high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized powder metallurgy processed alloy will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and improved ductility relative to alloys produced by conventional melting methods.
generation.baseline: Refractory HEAs produced via conventional melting, which typically are strong but exhibit brittle behavior due to coarse grains.
generation.boundary: Excessive milling may introduce contamination (such as oxides or carbides) that could negatively affect ductility, so the process parameters must be strictly controlled.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of strength and ductility improvement depends on the precise control of milling contamination and sintering conditions; further experimental optimization is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two alloy batches: one using conventional melting and one using the proposed powder metallurgy route (10-hour milling and SPS). Characterize microstructure by SEM/TEM for grain size and perform standardized mechanical tests to measure yield strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the powder metallurgy processed alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and ductility relative to the conventional melting route, the hypothesis will be falsified.

This fractional drop of HAGBs was also supported by the higher kernel average misorientation (KAM) values for the 350 and 650 RPM processed samples as compared to the as-homogenized microstructure. However, the KAM values were less than 1.2 irrespective of the processing condition, which also indicated the occurrence of dynamic recrystallization upon FSP. Moreover, most of the new grains were twin-free, and h.c.p ε was present in the form of plates within the f.c.c. grains as shown in Fig. 1b,c. Li et al., reported ~32% of h.c.p. phase in the microstructure with an average f.c.c. γ grain size of 4.5 μm upon cold-rolling and subsequent annealing at a furnace temperature of 900 °C for 3 min. After FSP we find that the same alloy showed ~8 and ~10% of h.c.p. at similar grain sizes of ~5.2 and 6.5 μm, respectively. Multi-component refractory elements-based alloys possess a mainly BCC structure. One of the most interesting HEA types is a system with coherent BCC and B2 phases with a microstructure similar to Ni-based alloys. The difference is that the disordered BCC phase is present as cubic nanoparticles. This structure provides a combination of high strength and high plasticity at high temperatures and is standard for Al-containing multi-component alloys. Thus, for the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, its yield strength is 745 MPa at 1000 °C, and good plasticity is preserved (the height decrease is >50% under compression) []. However, there can also be observed oxides and intermetallic phases, such as Laves phases, in the refractory HEAs that can affect the materials’ ductility. For example, in the NbCrMoTaTiZr, CrNbTiZr, and CrNbTiVZr alloys, the Laves phase is formed in the BCC-matrix because of the smaller radius of Cr in comparison to other elements [,,]. Nevertheless, in Reference [], an NbMoTaWVCr alloy with an extremely high yield strength of 3416 MPa and good plasticity of 5.3% at room temperature was obtained. This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials. Even though a protective atmosphere was used in the entire manufacturing process, carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.
